title: How Adobe’s Tech Lead Works and Uses AI
author: Gregor Ojstersek
summary: Gregor Ojstersek shares a case study from his O'Reilly book The Multiplier Mindset, profiling Navya Agarwal, a tech lead at Adobe. Agarwal says the technical side is about 40 percent of the role, and the rest is turning ambiguity into structure, asking uncomfortable questions early, and building what she calls the infrastructure of clarity through documentation, decision logs and careful reviews. The case study explains how she makes it safe to raise concerns, citing a launch delayed two weeks because a junior engineer flagged Android rendering problems, and how she multiplies others through clarity, documentation and deliberate restraint. She watches for the politeness trap, is transparent when scope and timeline do not fit, and rejects routine heroics as a symptom of broken planning. On AI, she uses it for first drafts and for enumerating failure modes while protecting judgment-heavy relational work, and she advises engineers to keep design, tests and review discipline. Her measure of success has shifted from what she builds to what the team becomes.
points: Agarwal frames psychological safety as a performance input, illustrated by a launch delay that avoided a broken experience for millions of users on lower-end Android devices.
The multiplier test is making the team less dependent on any one person, achieved through clarity, written documentation and the restraint to ask a question back rather than answer.
Asking a quieter engineer for her view first, before louder voices set the tone, helped her lead a key design review within two months.
Treating routine heroics as a planning failure leads to the aim of a boringly reliable team rather than one that runs in rescue mode.
AI raises the premium on judgment and clarity, so she uses it to draft and explore while insisting on design before code, tests alongside code, and the same review rigor for model output.
quotes: The biggest shift in Agarwal’s thinking has been moving away from the idea that her value is measured by how much code she personally writes.

Early in her career, impact felt like output. More features, more commits, more visible progress. As she grew into leadership, she realized that real leverage comes from helping other people do excellent work.
Tolerated means people can speak up but sense a slight friction when they do. Valued means the team treats early warnings as useful data, not as someone being difficult.
That gap between knowing something and feeling safe enough to say it is one of the most expensive gaps in engineering. My job, in that moment and in every moment like it, is to close it.
A multiplier,” she explains, “is not the person everyone depends on. A multiplier is the reason the team does not need to depend on any one person at all.
Heroic behavior is tempting because it is visible, and it comes from a genuine desire to own the outcome. But a team that depends on heroics to ship is a team whose planning is broken.
AI-generated code that nobody on the team truly understands is not an asset; it’s debt with a faster accumulation schedule.
Speed without clarity is just faster confusion. Use AI where it genuinely reduces friction on the right behaviors.
